title: Op straat
subtitle: Real-life Dutch for cafés, coffeeshops, shops and the market
intro: Practice for the conversations you'll actually have: ordering at the counter, the checkout questions, the cheese stall. Each place has a **role-play** where you answer out loud and the app listens, a **phrase sheet** to read before you walk in, and **curveballs** for when things go off script. Run each role-play a few times, because the shopkeeper's lines change every run.

survival.en: I'm learning Dutch. Can we keep it in Dutch?

survival.en: How do you say that in Dutch?

survival.nl: Dank u wel. / Dank je wel.

scenarios.title: In het café
scenarios.blurb: Order at the counter, sit down on a terras, ask for the bill.
tips: **Koffie** on its own is a black coffee. Want it milky? Say **koffie verkeerd**, literally 'coffee the wrong way round', the Dutch latte.
Order with **Mag ik een…?** or **Ik wil graag een…**. Plain **Ik wil een…** sounds blunt. **Doe maar een…** is relaxed and very Dutch.
In a sit-down café you order and pay at the table. Catch someone's eye and say **Mag ik afrekenen?** Rounding up is the normal tip: **Maak er maar tien euro van.**
Young city staff say **je**, so answer with je too. With older staff, start with **u**.
Looking for cannabis? That's a **coffeeshop**, which is a different place. See the coffeeshop scenario.

say.en: I'll have a koffie verkeerd (milky coffee).
Apple pie with whipped cream, please.

say.nl: Maak er maar tien euro van.
say.en: Make it ten euros (keep the change).

say.nl: Nee, dank je, dat was het.

hear.nl: Voor hier of om mee te nemen?
hear.en: For here or to take away?

hear.nl: Dat is dan vier euro vijftig.
Ga maar zitten, we brengen het.
hear.en: Take a seat, we'll bring it over.

scenarios.title: In de coffeeshop
scenarios.blurb: ID at the door, the menu, asking for something mild, the house rules.
tips: A **coffeeshop** sells cannabis. For coffee you want a **café** or **koffiebar**. Coffeeshops are 18+ only, and staff check your ID at the door, sometimes on every visit.
House rules: no more than **5 gram** per person per day, no alcohol, and **no tobacco indoors**. Joints are smoked pure or with a herbal mix (**kruiden**). A few cities only admit Dutch residents.
Be honest about strength. Say **Ik rook niet vaak** and staff will steer you to something milder. Edibles (**spacecake**) can take an hour or more to kick in, so wait before having more.
The menu is often behind the counter: **Mag ik de menukaart zien?** Many places are cash only, so check before you order. Sitting inside usually means buying a drink too.

scenarios.title: Bij de bakker
scenarios.blurb: Whose turn is it, half a loaf sliced, and pointing at things you can't name.
tips: Most bakeries have no ticket machine. Staff ask **Wie is er aan de beurt?** (Who's next?). If it's you, say **Ik!** or **Ik ben aan de beurt.**
Bread comes **heel** (whole) or **half** (half loaf), and they'll ask if you want it **gesneden** (sliced).
Bakery classics: **krentenbollen** (currant buns), **een gevulde koek** (almond-paste biscuit), **een tompouce** (pink-iced custard slice).
**Anders nog iets?** (anything else?) follows every item. **Nee, dat was het** ends the order.

scenarios.title: In de supermarkt
scenarios.blurb: Finding things, then the checkout's bonus card, bag and receipt questions.
tips: At the checkout (**de kassa**) you'll get the same three questions almost every time: **bonuskaart** (loyalty card, at Albert Heijn), **tasje** (bag), and **bonnetje** (receipt). Learn those three and you've got the checkout covered.
**Pinnen** means paying by debit card, and contactless is standard. Some places are card only (**alleen pin**).
To find something: **Waar kan ik … vinden?** or the more natural **Waar staat/staan …?** You'll hear **gangpad** (aisle), **achterin** (at the back), **bij de zuivel** (by the dairy).
You bag your own groceries, and bags aren't free.

scenarios.title: Op de markt
scenarios.blurb: Tasting cheese, a pound of this, two punnets for five, the 'bit more?' question.
tips: Weights: **een ons** = 100 g, **een pond** = 500 g, **een kilo**. You'll hear **twee ons** and **een half pond** all the time.
Gouda by age: **jong** (mild), **jong belegen**, **belegen**, **extra belegen**, **oud** (sharp, crumbly). Ask to taste: **Mag ik even proeven?**
The classic market line is **Mag het iets meer zijn?** The slice came out a bit heavy. **Ja, prima** is the normal answer.
Some stalls are cash only. Vendors talk fast and informally (**Zeg het maar!**, **Wie volgt?**), so don't hesitate to say **Iets langzamer, graag**.

scenarios.title: Drogist & apotheek
scenarios.blurb: Something for a sore throat, picking up a prescription, how often to take it.
tips: A **drogist** (Kruidvat, Etos) sells paracetamol, plasters and toiletries without a prescription. An **apotheek** fills prescriptions (**recepten**) sent by your huisarts.
Describe the problem with **Ik heb…** + **hoofdpijn / keelpijn / buikpijn**, or **Ik ben verkouden** (I have a cold). Then ask **Heeft u iets tegen…?**
At the apotheek they confirm your **geboortedatum** (date of birth). Practise saying yours, e.g. **twaalf maart negentienhonderdvijfennegentig**.
You'll often hear **Beterschap!** (get well soon) as you leave.

scenarios.title: In de kledingwinkel
scenarios.blurb: Just looking, another size, the fitting room, and exchanging something.
tips: Staff greet you with **Kan ik je ergens mee helpen?** The polite brush-off is **Nee, dank je, ik kijk even rond.**
Sizes: **maat S/M/L** for clothes (said *es, em, el*), **maat 42** for shoes and EU sizes. **Een maatje groter/kleiner** = one size up/down.
Fitting rooms are **de paskamers**. Fit words: **het past** (it fits), **te klein / te groot**, **te krap** (tight), **te wijd** (loose). **Hij staat je goed!** = it suits you.
Clothes are often **hij** (*de jas, de trui*): **Hoe zit hij?** means 'how does it fit?'. Returns need **de bon**. **Ruilen** = exchange, **een tegoedbon** = store credit.
